extracted.intended_audience: journalists, journalism educators, editors, and media-literate readers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of common patterns and red flags in journalistic fabrication/plagiarism cases, using the Ruth Shalit Barrett / Atlantic retraction as a case study. Intended to help reporters, editors, and educators recognize, prevent, and respond to journalistic fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and verifiability of factual details
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported facts (names, family details, injuries, locations, physical measurements) must be accurate and independently verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the Atlantic case: source's supposed son did not exist; described wounds did not match witness accounts; family placed in wrong city; exaggerated claim about 'Olympic-sized' rinks. Verify identifying details with multiple independent sources, corroborate physical descriptions (photos, medical records, eyewitnesses), and verify numerical/technical claims (e.g., rink dimensions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty with fact-checkers and editors
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must not mislead or deceive fact-checkers or editors, nor induce sources to lie during the verification process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Atlantic noted the author misled fact-checkers, lied to editors, and is accused of inducing at least one source to lie. Anti-pattern: coaching sources on what to say or concealing invented elements from fact-checking. Editorial policy should require transparency from writers about interview methods and any known uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough sourcing and independent corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should corroborate claims with multiple, independent sources rather than relying on a single account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Atlantic said its fact-checking spoke with more than 40 sources and independently corroborated information, yet still failed due to deception. Guidance: require independent lines of evidence for key claims (documents, on-the-record sources, physical evidence), and document the corroboration process in editorial files.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check author’s prior record for patterns of misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigate an author’s past for prior plagiarism, fabrication, or other ethical breaches since fraud is often repeated over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece stresses that fraudsters (e.g., Stephen Glass, Jayson Blair) had histories of misconduct. Use background checks, review prior work for red flags, and weigh past incidents when deciding to assign or trust a writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the necessity and proportionality of sensationalized details
rubrics_metrics.description: Be skeptical of colorful, sensational, or lurid details that add drama but little substantive value to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post notes many fabrications were 'unimportant crap'—coloring or spice added unnecessarily (Glass’s fanciful anecdotes, invented 'real people'). Ask whether a dramatic detail materially advances public knowledge; if not, demand stronger sourcing before publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heed newsroom 'spidey sense' and internal red flags
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay attention to colleagues’ complaints, unease, or anecdotal warnings about a reporter or a piece; these are often early indicators of problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include alumni and editors who earlier raised concerns about Blair and Glass. Encourage formal mechanisms to record and escalate internal concerns rather than dismissing them as sour grapes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutions must be prepared to correct and, when necessary, retract transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: When errors or deception are discovered, outlets should correct publicly, document the corrections, and retract if accuracy cannot be vouched for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Atlantic added corrective information on multiple dates before issuing a full retraction and an expanded editor’s note. Guidance: keep an audit trail of corrections, explain what failed and why, and be timely and transparent in apologies and retractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of cultural/institutional blindness to misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsrooms may rationalize or excuse dubious behavior (e.g., 'people can change' or speed pressures); this cultural bias can allow fraud to continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post explains why colleagues may ignore unease (loyalty, speed, disbelief that a colleague would lie). Countermeasures include formal checks, mandatory verification for high-risk claims, and training that normalizes raising concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating or fabricating sources, quotes, or 'real people' anecdotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not invent sources, quotes, or 'ordinary people' to provide flavor; these must be real and attributable (or properly anonymized with verification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mike Ward’s fabrication of 'regular people' and Glass’s invented characters are cited as common abuses. Require documented contact information and corroboration for anecdotal sources; flag unattributed color as high-risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure anonymization does not deanonymize or misidentify sources
rubrics_metrics.description: When protecting a source’s identity, anonymization techniques should not use details that make the person identifiable or introduce factual errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Atlantic case: the source was called by her middle name, which made her identifiable; also a son was invented. Guidance: verify that pseudonyms or withheld details actually protect identity and do not contradict other verified facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess motive and cost–benefit of fabrication
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider why an author might fabricate—often to feed ego or add sensational color rather than to advance important public interest—and evaluate the (lack of) journalistic justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post argues fabrications often fed egos and added nothing of value. Editors should question whether contested facts materially contribute to public knowledge and demand higher verification where motive to embellish exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize long-term reputational and career consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that discovered fabrication/plagiarism usually causes durable, often career-ending damage to the journalist and harms any outlet associated with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Janet Cooke, Stephen Glass, Jayson Blair had lasting fallout. Use this as a deterrent in ethics training and as context for disciplinary policies and rehabilitation decisions.
